title: Tenant Isolation Validation and Safe Migration Playbook
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Summary:

This playbook provides step-by-step validation checks and a safe migration approach for tenant isolation in Redwood Private deployments. It targets multi-tenant private clusters (VPC-hosted or on-prem) where tenant isolation must be demonstrably correct before accepting production traffic or performing stateful tenant migration. The document covers network microsegmentation, storage and KV isolation, GPU and scheduler tenancy, telemetry validation, rollback triggers, and post-migration acceptance tests.

Scope:

- Applies to private deployments with multi-tenant logical separation (namespaces, tenantIDs, or VRFs).
- Covers both greenfield tenant activation and migrating an existing tenant between control-plane groups or hardware pools.
- Day-2 validation and migration (not cluster bootstrap or hardware procurement).
- Non-goal: diving into vendor-specific hypervisor or switch firmware debug (see HW vendor runbooks).

Goals:

1) Provide a reproducible validation checklist that engineering and field teams can run.
2) Define a low-risk migration pattern that preserves in-flight KV/cache state and minimizes tokenized request latency spikes.
3) Specify observability signals and thresholds that gate migration and rollback.

Roles and ownership:

- Migration owner: eng-private-deployments field-engineering lead (primary contact for execution).
- Network lead: infra-networking (owns VPC routing, security groups, VRF).
- Storage lead: storage-and-fs team (owns NFS/EBS/Ceph policies).
- Runtime lead: serving-runtime (owns GPU scheduling, KV cache behavior).
- Onsite PO: customer success (schedules maintenance windows and acceptance).

Preconditions and assumptions:

- Tenant has a designated tenant ID and pre-provisioned quota in the target pool.
- Control-plane connectivity (API endpoint) between source and target regions is healthy.
- Key material rotated and validated (KMS access) for the target environment.
- Telemetry pipeline is available and historical baselines for the tenant exist (throughput, error rate, latency).

Validation checklist (high-level):

A. Networking and microsegmentation
- Verify tenant subnets/VRF are isolated: no cross-tenant TCP handshake allowed on internal service ports (7000-7999).
- Confirm security groups / NSGs permit only approved egress (destination CIDRs) and API control-plane access.
- Validate route tables for cross-zone failover are configured with precedence to preferred AZs.
- Test overlay policies (if using CNI + Cilium/Calico): policy deny-by-default is enforced for pod-to-pod traffic.

B. Identity and auth
- Confirm tenant-specific IAM roles map exactly to secrets in target KMS.
- Ensure service-account tokens are scoped and cannot call admin-level control-plane APIs.

C. Storage and state isolation
- Confirm tenant volumes provisioned with tenant-specific label and encryption key.
- Run read/write isolation test: tenant A cannot mount tenant B volumes; mount attempts must fail with EACCES.
- Verify KV namespace scoping: API returns 404 or namespace-not-found for cross-tenant key lookups.

D. KV cache and model cache tenancy
- Validate model KV cache TTLs and prefix segregation (prefixes must include tenantID).
- Run a cache-warm test for tenant and verify cache hit rate metrics are labeled with tenantID.

E. GPU compute and scheduler tenancy
- Confirm node labels and taints for tenant pools (e.g., node-role.kubernetes.io/tenant-<id>=true).
- Launch a synthetic workload that requests fractional GPUs; verify kube-scheduler and runtime allocate only from allowed nodes.

F. Quotas, billing tags, and accounting
- Validate that usage metrics attribute to the tenant tag and appear in cost reports within 5 minutes.

G. Observability and alerting
- Confirm per-tenant dashboards exist: p50/p95 generation latency, token rate, error rate, cache hit rate.
- Verify alert rules for tenant-level SLO breaches are firing in staging.

Validation tests (procedures):

1) Network isolation smoke test (5–15 minutes)
- From an isolated test pod in tenant A, attempt TCP connect to internal service IP of tenant B on 7123. Expected result: connection timeout or RST.
- From admin host, run: 
  curl -sS --connect-timeout 5 http://<tenant-b-internal-ip>:7123/health || echo "expected failure"
- Log: capture tcpdump (10s) showing no completed handshake.

2) Storage mount negative test (10 minutes)
- Attempt to mount tenant B’s PV into tenant A pod. Expected: permission denied.
- Command example: 
  kubectl run -i --rm --restart=Never mount-test --image=alpine -- /bin/sh -c "mount /dev/xvdh /mnt || echo \"mount failed expected\""

3) KV namespace enforcement (10 minutes)
- Use the tenant-scoped API to read a key from another tenant: expect 403/404.
- Example: 
  curl -H 'X-Tenant-ID: tenant-a' -X GET https://kv.example.internal/v1/key/tenant-b:customer_token

4) KV cache segregation and warm-up (20–30 minutes)
- Preload a model prefix for tenant into the target runtime. Confirm: /metrics shows cache_hit_total{tenant="tenant-a"} increasing.
- Confirm no cache spillover: cross-tenant cache_hit_total should remain zero.

5) GPU scheduling (20–30 minutes)
- Deploy a resource-heavy replica in the target tenant pool requiring GPUs. Validate allocation: 
  kubectl get pods -o wide --selector=app=synth-gpu-workload
- Confirm pod is scheduled only on nodes labeled tenant-target and that eviction thresholds are observed.

6) Telemetry and cost attribution smoke (15 minutes)
- Generate synthetic traffic at expected production rate for 5 minutes. Confirm per-tenant billing metrics appear within 5 minutes in the dashboard and that cost tags are present in raw metrics.

Safe migration strategy (recommended pattern):

Overview: The recommended migration pattern is a staged shadow-and-cutover with a small canary traffic window and sanity gating. It preserves in-memory KV where possible and falls back to source pool if acceptance tests fail.

Stage 0 — Preparation (T-24h to T-1h):
- Ensure backups and KV snapshot exports are successful and stored in customer-designated S3/Ceph bucket.
- Confirm all pre-migration validation tests pass in the target environment.
- Communicate maintenance window and rollback plan with customer success.

Stage 1 — Shadowing (T-60m):
- Start a shadow stream: mirror 1% of production requests to target while replies are ignored (no traffic cut).
- Verify telemetry parity (latency distribution and error taxonomy). Gate: if p95 latency regresses more than 30% or error rate increases >0.5% absolute, abort.

Stage 2 — Canary (T+0 to T+30m):
- Route 5–10% of low-risk traffic to target tenant. Maintain active read-through to source KV for writes where eventual consistency is acceptable.
- Run acceptance tests: end-to-end QA flows and TTL-driven batch jobs.

Stage 3 — Bulk cutover (T+30m to T+2h):
- If canary is healthy, increase traffic in controlled increments (25% -> 50% -> 75% -> 100%) with 10–15 minute observation windows.
- Monitor resource headroom and queue lengths.

Stage 4 — Finalization (T+2h onward):
- If 100% stable for 1 hour, mark migration complete: update billing tags, snapshot and prune source cache, and decommission source tenant allocations after configurable grace period (default 24h).

Rollback triggers and immediate actions:

- Trigger: p50/p95 generation latency > 2x baseline for 10 continuous minutes. Action: revert traffic routing to previous control-plane target (undo service mesh route, re-enable source gateway).
- Trigger: sustained error rate > 2% absolute. Action: pause cutover increments and roll back to last healthy traffic percentage; if not resolved within 10 minutes, full rollback.
- Trigger: data integrity mismatch in post-checks (missing keys or inconsistent outputs). Action: immediate rollback and engage storage lead for forensic snapshot.

Rollback procedure (high-level):

1) Disable new writes to target if state divergence suspected.
2) Re-route ingress (service mesh/router) back to source endpoints.
3) Re-point health-checks and load balancers to source.
4) Monitor source for steady state and verify metrics have returned to pre-migration baselines.

Acceptance tests (post-migration):

- E2E happy-path: 1 representative request-type completes within p95 latency threshold and correct business outputs.
- Regression set: run 50 curated eval prompts (prompt-set id: tenant-migration-smoke-2026) and confirm scoring parity with tolerance 0.5% QA metric delta.
- Data integrity: sample 100 keys written during migration and confirm parity in source snapshot.

Observability checklist (dashboards & signals):

- Per-tenant generation latency (p50/p90/p95) and token throughput.
- Runtime errors: OOM, CUDA errors, model decode failures.
- KV hit/miss rate by tenant.
- Network: SYN/FIN anomaly rate and connection resets per tenant.
- Billing: per-tenant cost increments with tags in time-series.

Appendix A — Useful commands and examples

- Simulate cross-tenant connection (from tenant A pod):
  kubectl exec -it test-pod -- /bin/sh -c "nc -vz <tenant-b-ip> 7123 || echo 'expected failure'"

- Snapshot KV (example):
  curl -X POST -H 'X-Admin-Token: <token>' https://kv-admin.internal/v1/snapshot?namespace=tenant-a

- Toggle service mesh route (istio example):
  kubectl apply -f canary-route.yaml  # route 10% to target
  kubectl apply -f full-route.yaml    # route 100% to target

Appendix B — Example migration gating matrix (human-readable table)

Gates (Pass criteria):
- Network isolation checks: PASS if 0 cross-tenant connections succeed in 5 attempts.
- Telemetry parity: PASS if median latency diff <= 20% and error delta <= 0.5% absolute.
- Storage integrity: PASS if 100 sampled keys are consistent.
- Billing attribution: PASS if cost tag appears in metric stream within 5 minutes.

If any gate fails, migration must stop and follow the rollback procedure.

Post-mortem and continuous improvement

- For every migration (successful or rolled back), create a migration post-mortem template with timestamps, gate results, and root cause for any failures. Retain and attach snapshots and raw telemetry to the post-mortem.
- Update this playbook with any newly discovered edge cases and add automated checks where possible.
